sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Describes two types of contracting approaches for micropile projects: (1) Method (procedural) approach — agency specifies all design, materials, and methods; agency assumes design risk; best for experienced agencies. (2) Performance approach — agency specifies geometric and performance requirements; contractor designs within those constraints; allows contractor innovation and often lower cost. Selection depends on agency experience, project complexity, and contractor availability. Both approaches are valid if properly implemented.
sections.body: The purpose of this chapter is to describe contracting approaches commonly used for projects involving micropiles. Two types of contracting methods are used to develop contract documents for micropile projects. Method (or Procedural) Approach: All details of design, construction materials, and methods are specified in the contract documents. The agency is fully responsible for the design and performance of the micropile, as long as the contractor has installed each component in strict accordance with the contract documents. The agency assumes all risks and is responsible for directing the work if changes are required based on actual field conditions. The use of a method specification is recommended only for agencies that have developed sufficient in-house expertise and consider micropile design and construction control as a conventional or standard method. Performance Approach: The agency specifies geometric requirements, material specifications, and performance requirements including factors of safety. The contractor designs the micropile within those constraints. Both approaches are valid if properly implemented; the selection may depend on the experience of the agency with micropile technology, the criticality and complexity of the project, and the availability of specialty contractors.
key_points: Method approach: agency specifies all details; agency assumes design risk; requires in-house expertise
Performance approach: agency specifies geometry and performance requirements; contractor designs
Both approaches are valid; selection depends on agency experience and project complexity
Method spec recommended only for agencies with sufficient in-house micropile expertise
Performance approach allows contractor innovation and potentially lower cost
Pre-qualification of specialty contractors is critical under either approach
sections.applicability: Selection of contracting approach for micropile foundation support and slope stabilization projects.

sections.title: Contractor Qualification
sections.summary: Pre-qualification of micropile contractors is critical for project success. Contract documents should define: (1) contractor pre-qualification requirements, (2) submittal procedures, and (3) enforcement methods. Recommended minimum requirements include number of years in business, number of completed micropile projects, and references. Agencies without prior micropile experience should seek a qualified third-party QA provider. Where formal pre-qualification is not allowed, bidders should demonstrate specific micropile experience.
sections.body: Because specialty geotechnical contractors are required for micropile work, the experience and qualifications of the contractor are critical to obtaining a satisfactory installation. The likelihood of success further increases when comprehensive construction quality assurance procedures are developed and enforced by the owner. Agencies or owners with no previous micropile experience should seek a qualified third-party quality assurance provider. Contract documents for micropile projects should clearly define: (1) the contractor pre-qualification requirements; (2) submittal procedures for this qualification information; and (3) the means by which the owner will enforce these requirements. Such pre-qualification requirements are commonly used by transportation agencies for other specialty construction techniques, such as permanent ground anchors, soil nail walls, drilled shaft foundations, and shotcreting. However, where formal pre-qualification may not be allowed, agencies should request that bidders demonstrate that they meet specific micropile experience requirements. Recommended minimum experience requirements typically include: minimum years in business, minimum number of completed micropile projects, minimum micropile footage installed, and client references.
key_points: Specialty contractor qualification is critical — micropile construction requires experienced firms
Contract documents must specify: pre-qualification requirements, submittal procedures, enforcement
Agencies with no micropile experience should use a qualified third-party QA provider
Minimum requirements typically: years in business, number of completed projects, footage installed, references
Where formal pre-qualification is not allowed, request proof of specific micropile experience from bidders
sections.applicability: Setting contractor qualification requirements for micropile project contracts.

sections.title: Method Contracting Approach
sections.summary: Three variants of the method (owner-controlled design) contracting approach: (1) Standard Design — owner provides design loads, footing design, and layout; contractor designs micropile cross-section and bond length. Bidding on preliminary design, detailed design submitted after award. Payment per pile or per lineal meter plus add/deduct for rock footage. (2) Alternate Micropile Design — owner provides primary design; contractor may propose alternate. (3) Cost Reduction Incentive (Value Engineering) — contractor proposes savings after award; savings shared between owner and contractor.
sections.body: The method contracting approach involves owner-controlled design where the agency or owner's engineer provides the micropile design loadings, footing design, and pile layout for foundation support. The contractor provides the micropile design (cross-section and bond length) and pile top to footing connection design. This division allows qualified specialty contractors to provide an economical micropile design while satisfying design requirements, and allows responsibility to be shared between the owner and the micropile contractor. Three variants are described: Standard Design Type: contract documents allow for various qualified micropile designs. Owner provides geotechnical reports, design loadings, footing geometry, and constraints. Contractor provides preliminary design during bidding and detailed design calculations and working drawings after contract award for review and approval. Payment is recommended on a unit-per-micropile basis for: (1) furnished and installed production piles; (2) verification testing; and (3) proof testing, with an add/deduct footage price for piles founded in rock. Alternate Micropile Design: owner provides a primary design that bidders must price; contractors may also propose an alternate design. Cost Reduction Incentive (Value Engineering): allows contractors to propose cost savings after award, typically splitting savings between owner and contractor. Timely review and approval is critical since foundation support elements are usually first order of work.
key_points: Standard Design: owner provides loadings and layout; contractor provides micropile cross-section and bond length design
Contractor submits preliminary design at bidding; detailed design after award for review/approval
Payment: per pile (production), per each (verification/proof tests), add/deduct footage for rock
Alternate Micropile Design: owner provides primary design; alternate design may be submitted
Value Engineering: contractor proposes savings post-award; savings split with owner
Owner assumes design risk under method specifications
sections.applicability: Agency-controlled design contracting approach for micropile projects; appropriate when agency has sufficient in-house expertise.

sections.title: Performance Specifications
sections.summary: The performance (line and grade) approach has the agency prepare drawings defining geometric requirements and material specifications, define performance requirements including factors of safety, and indicate the range of acceptable construction methods. The contractor designs the system. Benefits include contractor use of proprietary equipment, reduced engineering cost, and innovation. Contractor specifies: construction process, micropile type and quantity, micropile design, footing detail revisions, and connection design. Bid proposal submitted pre-bid or post-bid; payment typically lump sum.
sections.body: This approach is often called 'line and grade' or 'conceptual plans.' Under this approach, the agency: (1) prepares drawings defining the geometric requirements for the structure and material specifications for the components; (2) defines performance requirements including factors of safety; and (3) indicates the range of acceptable construction and design methods. This approach, when coupled with sound specifications and pre-qualification of contractors, offers several benefits. Design of the structure is performed by trained and experienced staff and can utilize contractors' proprietary equipment and methods along with material components successfully and routinely used in the past. Also, the performance specification approach lessens engineering costs for the owner. The micropile contractor specifies: micropile construction process, micropile type and quantity, micropile design, revisions to footing details to accommodate the micropile design, and pile top to footing connection design. Based upon specified limitations and requirements, a design/build proposal is submitted, either before bid advertisement (pre-bid) or after contract award (post-bid). Measurement and payment is typically made on a lump-sum basis. Performance requirements provided by the owner typically include: micropile design loadings, geometric requirements, design criteria and parameters, micropile testing procedures, instrumentation requirements, special design considerations (scour, liquefaction), and performance criteria.
key_points: Agency specifies: geometry, material specs, performance requirements (FS), acceptable methods
Contractor specifies: construction process, micropile type/quantity, design, connection details
Benefits: allows contractor proprietary methods, reduced owner engineering cost, innovation
Design/build proposal submitted pre-bid or post-bid; payment typically lump sum
Performance requirements include: loadings, geometry, design criteria, test requirements, special considerations
sections.applicability: Performance-based contracting for micropile projects where contractors have proprietary methods and agency has less in-house expertise.

sections.title: Design/Build Approach
sections.summary: In design/build contracting, the specialty contractor is part of the project team and responsible for adequacy of both design and construction. The owner provides: structure loadings, geotechnical data, design criteria, site constraints, and acceptance criteria. The contractor submits preliminary design at bidding and detailed design after award. Subcontracted items are bid by specialty firms. After award, the contractor begins work immediately without a separate design review phase. Payment is lump sum. Two variants: post-bid design (post-award design review) and pre-bid design (full design at bidding).
sections.body: In design/build construction, the specialty contractor becomes an important part of the project team and is involved in all foundation and ground-support aspects of the project. The micropile contractor is responsible for the adequacy of the design and construction. The owner provides: geotechnical reports and data; structure loadings (axial, lateral, and moment); existing utility drawings; design criteria and parameters; site limitations (e.g., right of way); design and details of ancillary structures; contractor working drawing/design submittal and review requirements; and micropile acceptance criteria. During the bidding process, micropile contractors prepare a preliminary design and a firm cost proposal based on the owner's plans and specifications. For subcontracted items, general contractors receive bids from specialty subcontractors and include the best cost proposals in their bids. Once the contract is awarded, the selected specialty contractor prepares detailed design calculations and working drawings and submits them to the engineer for review and approval. Post-bid design: contractor submits detailed design after award for review before construction begins. Pre-bid design: contractor submits complete design at the time of bidding, allowing the owner to evaluate design quality in addition to cost.
key_points: Contractor responsible for adequacy of both design and construction
Owner provides: loadings, geotechnical data, design criteria, site constraints, acceptance criteria
Preliminary design at bidding; detailed design submitted after award for review/approval
Two variants: post-bid design (review before construction) and pre-bid design (full design at bid)
General contractor includes specialty subcontractor in bid; specialty firm named in bid
After award, construction can begin once detailed design is approved
sections.applicability: Design/build contracting approach for micropile projects where the contractor takes full design and construction responsibility.

sections.title: Contract Plans
sections.summary: Contract plans must include sufficient information for contractors to prepare competitive bids meeting the owner's objectives. Critical elements: quality of subsurface information, existing utility plan, and micropile design criteria. Conservative design criteria and inadequate subsurface data create expensive contingencies, higher prices, and claim potential. Sample contract plans are provided in Appendix C-1 (owner-controlled design methods) and Appendix C-2 (contractor design/build methods).
sections.body: For all specification methods, the contract plans must include sufficient information to allow the contractor to develop a bid proposal that meets the owner's objectives. The quality of the subsurface information, existing utility plan, and micropile design criteria are very important for a successful project. Inadequate subsurface information and overly conservative pile design criteria may create expensive contractor contingencies, higher pile prices, and increase claim potential. In contrast, comprehensive subsurface information reduces uncertainty and allows contractors to provide more competitive and accurate bids. Sample contract plans and guide construction specifications utilizing owner controlled design methods are provided in Appendix C-1. Sample contract plans and guide specifications utilizing contractor design/build methods are provided in Appendix C-2.
key_points: Contract plans must provide sufficient information for competitive bidding
Inadequate subsurface data and conservative criteria lead to contingency pricing and claims
Good subsurface data reduces contractor uncertainty and produces more competitive bids
Appendix C-1: sample plans for owner-controlled design specifications
Appendix C-2: sample plans for contractor design/build specifications
sections.applicability: Preparing contract plan requirements for micropile projects regardless of contracting approach.
